cards.title: Footer text block to offset image-heavy emails
cards.summary: Pad image-heavy campaigns with invisible footer text to reduce spammy image-to-text ratios in Gmail's eyes.
cards.use_when: Before scheduling a design-heavy campaign or hero-image email that contains little body copy, when you want to reduce the risk of promotions/spam placement.
steps: Recognize the pattern the source flags: if an email is mostly images with only a few lines of text, this can look 'fishy' to Gmail.
Found a campaign that uses almost no text? Compensate by adding a large block of real prose (the source copies a brand's About Us page) at the bottom of the email.
In the email builder, add a text block at the very bottom, paste the text, and center it.

Style it to be effectively invisible: set font size very small (the source uses size five), set font color to the same color as the background, and reduce line spacing (the source uses about 5%) so it consumes almost no vertical space.
Confirm the block is invisible in both desktop and mobile previews before sending.
Send a test preview to yourself and check layout, links and rendering before scheduling.
caveats: Presented by the source as a trick it likes to use, not a guaranteed deliverability fix; hidden text can itself be treated as a spam signal by some filters, so treat as an experiment and monitor placement.
Only use text you have the right to reuse (the source copies another brand's About page content, which is not advisable for your own commercial emails).

cards.title: Link and alt-text pass before a campaign goes out
cards.summary: Finish every email by wiring all image/button links and writing alt text, then test-send before scheduling.
cards.use_when: Final QA step on any campaign, after copy and design are done and before scheduling the send.
steps: Walk the email top to bottom and link every clickable element to the correct destination: the source links the main hero to the brand's home page, one section to the blog, and collection sections to the men's and women's category pages.
Match each link to the section's intent rather than defaulting everything to the homepage.
Add alt text to each image, briefly paraphrasing the message (the source's example: 'top no-fuss dumbbell back exercises').
Note that image blocking affects a very small share of recipients (source says under 1%), so alt text is secondary but quick to add.
Send yourself a test email and click every link, then check desktop and mobile rendering.
Only then schedule or send the campaign.
caveats: The source states alt text may sometimes help deliverability but is 'really not a big deal' — don't treat it as a major ranking lever.
Exact button locations and preview options in your ESP may change; verify in the current interface.

cards.title: Treat deliverability as a sender reputation score
cards.summary: Inbox providers rank you like a credit score: good reputation lands in primary, bad lands in spam, mediocre lands in promotions.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing why campaigns aren't being seen, or when deciding whether low revenue is a content problem or a placement problem.
steps: Frame deliverability as your domain/IP 'credit score' — the question is whether you land in primary, promotions or spam.
Understand the provider's incentive: inbox providers only surface emails users want so users keep using the platform; they watch engagement as the signal.
Use open and click engagement as the practical proxy: if few people open or click, providers push you toward promotions or spam, which further reduces visibility — a self-reinforcing cycle.
Check the technical layer first: the source says if your ESP (e.g., Klaviyo) shows no warning at the top of the homepage about domain setup, assume technical requirements are already in place.
If technicals are fine, split the cause into two: either your emails are weak, or your sender reputation is poor and you are being filtered.
caveats: The credit-score framing is the source's analogy, not an official metric.
The source's claim that a clean ESP dashboard means you're fine is a simplification — authentication and domain setup still deserve a direct check.

cards.title: Improve the emails before chasing technical fixes
cards.summary: The source's number-one deliverability lever is simply sending better, more varied, engaging email content.
cards.use_when: When open rates are low and you're tempted to look for technical hacks instead of fixing the content your list receives.
steps: Accept the source's framing: low engagement has two causes — emails people don't want to open, or poor sender reputation from placement.
Attack the content side first: the source calls sending better content the number-one lever it sees for deliverability gains.
Avoid the templated look: the source warns against 'send the same templated BS' where you drop a product into a template in five minutes with no clear value to the reader.
Instead vary the topic and format each send so opening gives a small reward — the source describes this as a dopamine loop where a good past email makes the next open more likely.
Use a clean design and genuinely good copy, and give people a reason to look forward to the send.
Keep the format varied (the source sends different topics and layouts rather than one repeated template).
caveats: This is the presenter's opinion grounded in agency experience, not a controlled benchmark.
Improved content still won't help if authentication and reputation basics are broken.

cards.title: Build 14/30/60/90-day engaged segments
cards.summary: Create rolling engagement segments defined by opens or clicks in the last 14, 30, 60 and 90 days, excluding bounces.
cards.use_when: Setting up the segment structure before running a deliverability recovery, or before deciding who should be in your base sending list.
steps: In your ESP segment builder, create four segments keyed on recency: opened or clicked in the last 14, 30, 60 and 90 days.
Include an OR condition: opened email at least once in the window OR clicked email at least once in the window — the source adds this because click tracking can register without an open being logged.
Add a subscribed condition so only marketable contacts are included.
Add a condition requiring zero bounced emails.
Repeat the same structure for each window so the segments nest: 14-day inside 30-day inside 60-day inside 90-day.
Use these four segments as the gating logic for every campaign you send during recovery.
caveats: The source notes click tracking can be unreliable in some ESPs, so the OR condition is a fail-safe rather than a perfect measure.
Window lengths are the source's heuristics; adapt to your list size and send frequency.

cards.title: Six-week deliverability recovery protocol
cards.summary: Warm reputation back by sending only to tight engaged segments, then expanding as open rates hold.
cards.use_when: When campaigns are landing in spam/promotions and you want a structured plan to regain primary inbox placement.
steps: Weeks 1–3: build the 14/30/60/90-day engaged segments, and turn off all automated flows except the high-engagement ones — welcome, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon and post-purchase. The source argues these are opened at a high clip (people want their discount, their cart reminder, their order info) and therefore boost credibility.
Weeks 1–3 onward: send three highly engaging campaigns per week to only the 14-day engaged list. The source argues sending one per week just stretches the same recovery over three times as long.
Expand only when earned: once the 14-day segment is consistently at 50%+ opens for three straight campaigns, add the 30-day segment at three sends per week.
Weeks 5–6: keep monitoring opens; if you dip below roughly 40–50%, tighten back to the smaller segment.
Continue expanding to the 60-day segment as opens hold near 50%, then to the 90-day segment.
Week 6+: treat the 90-day engaged list as your base sending list, and send one campaign per month to the full newsletter list to try to re-activate dormant contacts.
caveats: The 40–50% and 50%+ thresholds and the three-per-week cadence are the source's own heuristics from agency work, not industry standards.
Opening to the full list monthly works only if that campaign is genuinely engaging; the source says it can just be a normal email.
The source states its main client case went from the 20–30% open range to about 60% opens after roughly 60 days — a single example, not a promise.

cards.title: Keep only high-engagement flows during recovery
cards.summary: Pause most automations and lean on welcome, abandon and post-purchase flows, which reliably earn high engagement.
cards.use_when: Deciding which automations to leave running while rebuilding sender reputation, or which flows to prioritize when you can't build everything at once.
steps: Turn off all flows except: welcome, browse abandonment, cart abandonment, checkout abandonment and post-purchase.
Keep the welcome flow because contacts just opted in for a discount and will open the first email delivering it.
Keep cart and checkout abandonment because the reminder about an item they were already considering earns strong engagement.
Keep post-purchase because customers want order information.
Understand why this matters during recovery: every send that gets opens and clicks is a vote of confidence with providers; flows generate those votes without needing new campaign content.
Re-enable the remaining flows once engagement and placement have recovered.
caveats: This is the source's recommended recovery posture, not a claim that other flows are worthless.
If a flow's own engagement is weak for your brand, including it dilutes the signal you're trying to send.

cards.title: Three-to-four campaigns per week as your default cadence
cards.summary: Send 3–4 campaigns weekly to your engaged list to stay top of mind, provided the content is genuinely good.
cards.use_when: Setting your ongoing campaign frequency after recovery, or testing whether your current once-a-week rhythm is too thin.
steps: Adopt 3–4 campaigns per week to the engaged list as the default — the source reports this as the sweet spot in roughly 90% of the cases it has tested.
Accept the reasoning: if you send one email a week, people forget you and engagement decays.
Recognize the conditional: the source explicitly says if your emails are bad, 3–4 per week is too much; frequency only works when content is good.
Treat it as a compounding loop — good send, engagement, recognition, more engagement — rather than a one-off tactic.
Watch open and click rate on the engaged segments; if engagement collapses, the lever to pull is tighter segments and better content, not necessarily fewer sends.
caveats: The '90% of cases' figure is the presenter's own estimate from client work.
This cadence is asserted as opinion based on generated revenue; it is not a study and will not hold for brands with weak content or tiny lists.

cards.title: Text-based emails vs graphic emails A/B test
cards.summary: Test pure-text campaigns against graphic campaigns; the source's example showed text winning on clicks and placed orders.
cards.use_when: Planning a weekly A/B test, especially for a best-sellers or product roundup campaign where you'd default to heavy graphics.
steps: Set up a split test where variant A is a fully graphic email (product imagery, banners) and variant B is a text-based email with no product imagery.
Run it on a campaign type where you assume graphics are required — the source's example was a best-sellers email, where the text version outperformed.
Reason about why text can win: almost everyone sends graphics, so plain text stands out in a crowded inbox.
Use the results to decide where text fits in your ongoing mix rather than replacing graphics entirely.
The source recommends keeping both formats in rotation and using each where it performs.
caveats: The source presents one brand's example results (text version showed roughly 50% better click rate and more placed orders) as an illustration, not a guaranteed outcome.
Results will vary by brand and audience — the source explicitly says to test rather than assume.

cards.title: Judge subject-line tests on placed orders, not opens
cards.summary: Subject line can shift purchase behavior; measure its A/B test on placed order rate and revenue, not just open rate.
cards.use_when: Running subject-line tests on campaigns or abandonment emails, and deciding which subject line to roll out.
steps: Run the subject-line test as a proper split on the same email body.

Read the open rate as a check but make the decision on placed order rate and order value — the source's abandonment example had nearly identical opens (the higher-open variant was slightly ahead) yet 11.6% vs 3.8% placed order rate.

Test emotional framing: the source contrasts something lower-barrier like 'your order is ready to go / packed and ready, just click' against something like 'your order's waiting for you', and reports lower barrier-to-entry language driving the higher placed order rate.
Test an exclusivity angle too, since the source says subject lines can affect whether and how someone buys.
Repeat subject-line tests frequently (the source frames these as weekly tests), not once a month, and log placed order rate as the primary metric.
caveats: The specific 11.6% vs 3.8% figures come from one anonymized brand test and are not benchmarks.
Attribution on open rate can be noisy; the source itself notes open-rate differences may be variability.

cards.title: Products vs categories in the email body
cards.summary: Test showing individual products against linking to category pages; higher-SKU brands may find individual products win.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to merchandise a campaign for a catalog with many SKUs — show specific products or send people to browse a category.
steps: If you sell many SKUs, run this test early with a client/brand, because the result shapes how you merchandise emails going forward (the source says it tests this very early).
Variant A: show or link categories — e.g., men's vs women's, or a category hub page.
Variant B: show individual products directly in the email (e.g., four men's products, four women's products).
The source's working hypothesis was that categories would win for a high-SKU store, but the test showed individual products had a higher click rate (1.14% vs 1.04%) and far more purchases.
Reason about why: when you give shoppers many category options they must keep searching; showing the product directly shortens the path.
Skip this test for single-product stores, and remember the outcome can flip by brand — the source says it sees both directions.
caveats: The source reports only one brand's numbers and notes another brand could see categories win.
The source declines to attribute the higher average order value to the email itself.

cards.title: Long-form vs short-form email body copy
cards.summary: Test longer founder-story copy against a few lines of text with a clear CTA; short won in the source's welcome-flow test.
cards.use_when: Writing a welcome-flow email or any campaign where you're tempted to explain product science, origin story or background at length.
steps: Create variant A: long form, e.g., a note from the founder explaining why the product is good, with substantial background and product detail.
Create variant B: short form — the source's example was about six lines: a warm welcome, one interesting product fact, and a shop-now CTA.
Run both on a meaningful sample (the source's example used ~2,000 recipients per side) and read click rate and placed order rate.
In the source's test, the long version produced 2.4% clicks and a 0.2% placed order rate, while the short version produced 3.4% clicks and a 0.7% placed order rate.
Reason: people don't read every word; long copy buries the call to action, while short copy keeps the CTA visible.
Roll out the winner for that audience but keep testing, since the source notes the right length differs by audience.
caveats: One brand's test result; not a rule that short always wins.
The source's sample-size disclosure (~2,000 each side) is what it used to argue the result wasn't accidental — your own significance needs depend on your volumes.

cards.title: Test send time of day for campaigns
cards.summary: Morning vs late-afternoon sends can swing engagement sharply; dial in your brand's best window.
cards.use_when: After you've settled cadence and content, when tuning when campaigns actually go out.
steps: Set up a same-day time split on a campaign — the source's example compared roughly 11 a.m. against 4 p.m.
Read open rate, click rate and placed order rate; the source's example showed 36% opens in the morning vs 26% in the late afternoon, with placed orders much higher earlier in the day.
Don't assume the intuitive answer: the source notes people often assume evenings or late afternoon work because shoppers are off work, but in its test the lunchtime-ish window performed better.
Account for the sample issue: the source cautions there were too few placed orders at the lower-performing time to lean on that metric alone.
Once you identify a better window, apply it persistently — the source frames the payoff as a fixed uplift per campaign that compounds over months.
Re-test occasionally, since the best window is brand-specific.
caveats: One brand's timing test with a thin placed-order sample; the source says results depend on the brand.
Send-time tools and inbox behavior change; verify how your ESP handles time-zone splits.

cards.title: Test flow delay timing for site abandonment
cards.summary: A 30-minute reminder isn't always better than a 4-hour one — test delays in abandonment flows on placed order rate.
cards.use_when: Setting the delay on a browse/site abandonment flow or any reminder email where you've assumed 'strike while the iron is hot'.
steps: Set up a test on the flow's first delay: variant A sends around 30 minutes after abandonment, variant B waits about 4 hours.

Use the source's example as the hypothesis to challenge: the 30-minute version was assumed to be better because the visit was fresh, but it produced a much lower placed order rate (0.7%) than the 4-hour version, on a large sample.
Read engagement carefully: the fast version had fewer opens and clicks, which the source interprets as people not being ready yet; the later send reached them when they had time to buy.
Consider the context explanation: someone who abandons may be busy with kids or errands and still busy 30 minutes later, but settled in bed at night when the 4-hour reminder arrives.
Apply the same testing discipline to delays between later messages in the flow, not just the first email.
caveats: This is one brand's flow test; the source says delays will differ per flow and must be tested.
Placed order rate on a flow depends on attribution windows — verify how your ESP attributes flow revenue.

cards.title: Branded text email vs plain native text email
cards.summary: Once you choose text-based sends, test a branded version (logo header/footer) against a fully plain native-format email.
cards.use_when: Executing text-based campaigns and deciding whether to include your logo and footer or send truly plain text.
steps: Define variant A — branded text: plain text body with your logo at the top (clickable, driving site visits) and your footer at the bottom, giving brand association.

Define variant B — plain text: nothing but text, rendered in the inbox provider's native format (white background, black text, like an email from a friend), usually a bit shorter and easier to digest.

Run the test and compare delivered volume, click rate and placed order rate; the source's example had 1,900 delivered on branded vs 1,400 on plain, similar revenue, but plain showed a higher placed order rate (1.7% vs 1.2%) and higher click rate (4% vs 3%).
Choose per message intent: the source suggests plain/perceived-personal for founder-voice emails ('hey, it's Max, the founder'), and branded text when the message comes from the brand itself.
Keep both in your rotation and lean toward the one performing better for your list.
caveats: One brand's test with modest delivered volumes; the source notes results depend on the brand and message.
The plain-text version sacrifices the clickable logo, which can cost some site traffic.

cards.title: Weekly A/B test roster of high-leverage variables
cards.summary: Keep a standing list of high-leverage email variables and test one deliberately every week rather than tweaking two words monthly.
cards.use_when: Building a recurring experimentation plan for your email program so testing keeps producing revenue rather than becoming sporadic.
steps: Treat these as your roster of high-leverage variables to work through: graphic vs text-based email; subject lines; products vs categories; long vs short form; campaign send time; flow delay timing; branded vs plain text.
Run them as real splits on meaningful samples — the source criticizes one-off 'change two words once a month' tests as not enough to maximize revenue.
Read the right metric per test: placed order rate and revenue for subject lines, products-vs-categories and flow timing; click rate plus placed order rate for format and length tests.
Rotate through the roster so each variable actually gets tested for your brand instead of assumed.
Log results and roll the winner into the standing program, then re-test periodically since audiences shift.
caveats: The source lists these variables from its own agency practice; they're a prioritization, not an exhaustive or statistically rigorous framework.
Small lists will struggle to reach significance on split tests — the source's own examples lean on ~2,000-per-side samples.

cards.title: Prime an LLM with brand context before writing email copy
cards.summary: Feed the model exhaustive brand, product, customer and voice information first so later copy prompts have real context.
cards.use_when: Setting up an AI-assisted email copy workflow for a store before generating any campaign copy.
steps: Write a priming prompt that dumps in as much brand information as possible: what you sell, mission, brand story, what makes the brand unique, ideal customer, brand voice, goals and aspirations.
Use full paragraphs rather than quick sentences — the source stresses giving it as much space and information as you can.
Include the store's website link so the model can pull additional context from it.
Keep this priming block reusable so every subsequent copy prompt in the session inherits the same context.
Expect the model to need product-level facts (materials, positioning, specific product copy) closer to when you draft.
caveats: The source's example primer for a large apparel brand is described as 'pretty brief' — more is generally better.
Model behavior and supported features change; verify what your current tool does with links and long prompts.

cards.title: Prompt for graphic-email copy structure, then iterate
cards.summary: Ask for graphic-campaign copy with a punchy headline, subheadline and short body leading to a shop-now CTA, then refine across several rounds.
cards.use_when: Drafting hero and body copy for a graphic campaign and you want structured output instead of a wall of generic AI prose.
steps: State the format explicitly: 'we're creating a graphic based email campaign with minimal copy to send to our customers' — the source says without 'graphic based' the model returns letter-style text.
State the topic in plain language, including the emotional angle (e.g., best sellers as your MVP in the gym, helping you break PRs).
Request a 'quick and punchy' headline — the source says without 'punchy' you get a 20-word headline.
Request a slightly longer subheadline plus 2–3 sentences of body copy leading into a shop-now CTA, mirroring the hero structure of headline → subheadline → body → button.
Treat the first output as a draft: iterate ('make it more unique', 'make the headline more conversational', 'give me more options for headlines') and combine your favorite fragments.
Do the final polish yourself — the source treats the model as a support player, not the finisher, and reports this is how its agency writes copy.
caveats: The source warns AI copy is recognizable via clichés ('you're in luck', 'crafting', 'enthusiasts', 'we're diving into the exciting world', 'unleash your potential') and should not be shipped as-is.
Prompt phrasing effectiveness is model- and version-dependent.

cards.title: Generate a year of non-discount email topics from micro-topics
cards.summary: Use a macro-to-micro prompt to produce broad themes and specific subtopics that become a full year of educational, non-discount campaigns.
cards.use_when: Planning a campaign calendar and running out of non-discount angles, especially for niche or technical product categories.
steps: Write a prompt stating the niche, what you sell, your brand mission/benefits, your average customer and what they want.
Ask for 10 overarching, general topics that tie into product benefits and customer lives.

Ask for 10 very specific subtopics under each overarching topic, written to educate the customer and potentially position your product as a solution — the source's prompt produced roughly 100 usable ideas.

Treat the output as raw material: for a supplement brand the source got themes like holistic health and wellness, sustainable muscle building and the science of natural supplements, with subtopics like adaptogens and stress, sleep and muscle recovery, gut health, and mental health and fitness.
Turn each promising subtopic into one campaign, and let brand-specific angles you think of yourself take priority over the AI list.
Feed the best ideas into your 3–4-per-week cadence so non-discount content fills most of the calendar.
caveats: Output quality varies — the source notes some generated topics needed cleanup.
The source insists AI is only a starting point and should never be the sole source of your content.
